The proliferation of host-microbiome multi-omics studies across nearly every major disease area has made integration a defining methodological challenge of contemporary systems biology. In pulmonary disease, integrative analyses of bulk, single-cell and spatial transcriptomics with peripheral blood profiling have supported a causal gut–immune–lung axis in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis through Mendelian randomization and nominated a four-gene signature comprising CXCL13, IL33, TLR4 and IGF1 [R5]. Cardiovascular research has interrogated six microbiome and eight host blood transcriptomic datasets to identify microbe–metabolite–host gene tripartite associations in atherosclerosis, although the authors themselves flag methodological heterogeneity and the lack of consensus signatures across studies [R6]. Neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative disorders are following the same trajectory: integrative 16S, metaproteomic, metabolomic and host proteomic profiling in thirty children with severe autism and controls has linked Tyzzerella enrichment and Bifidobacterium- and Klebsiella-derived metaproteins to altered neurotransmitters [R7], while in Alzheimer's disease the combination of plasma proteomics, metabolomics and gut and saliva metagenomics from 87 well-phenotyped patients has yielded composite predictors of dementia severity, including SKAP1, NEFL, homovanillate, glutamate and Paraprevotella clara, validated through artificial-intelligence-based models [R9]. Oncology is not far behind: parallel microbial, transcriptomic and metabolomic profiling of tumour and adjacent tissue from 50 glioma patients has connected intratumoral bacteria to synapse-associated host genes and to bacterial-associated metabolites through mediation analysis [R8]. Even within a single condition, the inflammatory bowel disease and irritable bowel syndrome literatures demonstrate that cross-cohort integration of nine metagenomic and four metabolomic cohorts [R10], multi-omic profiling of 495 subjects [R11] and longitudinal integration of microbiome, metabolome, epigenome and transcriptome layers in an application cohort [R12] are now considered baseline rather than exceptional.

Yet the operational reality beneath this descriptive success is sobering. The label "multi-omics" is still routinely applied to studies in which each layer is analysed independently and the results tabulated side by side rather than modelled jointly. In several of the examples above, integration is reduced to correlation of pre-computed feature lists, mediation testing of a handful of candidates, or machine-learning classifiers trained on concatenated matrices, none of which formally captures the dependence structures that motivate multi-omics in the first place. The intellectual leap from parallel inspection to joint inference is non-trivial, and the methodological pluralism is large enough that the field is recognisably constrained by methodological heterogeneity across studies [R6], by inconsistent sample coverage and heterogeneous data formats [R1] and by the absence of consensus signatures [R6]. Reproducibility is correspondingly fragile: re-running a published pipeline against the same inputs frequently yields divergent conclusions because data wrangling, normalisation, transformation and feature-selection choices are buried in bespoke scripts and undocumented parameter settings, with no widely adopted container, dependency-pinning, workflow-manager or test-coverage conventions enforced across the integration literature. The result is a literature in which impressive cohort sizes and sophisticated wet-lab procedures sit atop surprisingly fragile computational infrastructure.

This is the software gap that purpose-built integration tooling must address. Single-omics pipelines are exquisitely tuned for their own assays but offer no principled way to harmonise feature spaces, handle missing modalities, align longitudinal sampling or propagate uncertainty across layers. Several frameworks occupy parts of this niche. The Analyst suite provides web-based entry points for single-omics analysis, knowledge-driven network integration and data-driven joint dimensionality reduction across transcriptomics, proteomics, lipidomics and metabolomics [R3]. timeOmics extends the Bioconductor ecosystem with a generic framework for longitudinal multi-modal data, including pre-processing, modelling and clustering [R4]. Outside analysis itself, SUMO targets the benchmarking deficit by simulating multi-omics datasets with controllable latent structure and noise [R2]; simulation is methodologically necessary but cannot substitute for an end-to-end workflow. Among more widely used engines outside the present evidence base, MOFA and its successors, mixOmics with its supervised extension DIABLO, the nf-core pipeline collections, and microbiome-oriented platforms such as Anvi'o, QIIME 2 and TreeSummarizedExperiment all occupy adjacent niches in the broader integration ecosystem, but their detailed comparison with EMP lies beyond what the available evidence base can adjudicate. Within microbiome research specifically, EasyMultiProfiler (EMP) is a recent workflow that organises microbiome multi-omics analysis into five modules — data extraction, preparation, support, analysis and visualisation — built on the SummarizedExperiment and MultiAssayExperiment data classes [R1]. EMP provides an explicit microbiome focus, but its scope does not extend to a general solution to multi-omics integration.

That scope limitation can be specified in terms of the four tools for which evidence is available. The Analyst suite, timeOmics, SUMO and EMP are not direct functional peers: the Analyst suite is web-based and oriented toward transcriptomics, proteomics, lipidomics and metabolomics rather than microbiome data; timeOmics is restricted to longitudinal designs; SUMO is a simulator rather than an end-to-end pipeline; and EMP is the only microbiome-specific workflow in the set. Within EMP's own scope, its outputs remain conditional on the curated defaults and example datasets it ships with, and no peer-reviewed evidence in the present base has benchmarked these defaults against alternatives — a caveat that, in different forms, applies to every framework above but is rarely quantified in the original reports. The prior ecosystem has not yet addressed microbiome-specific needs with the same depth it has brought to single-omics or to general multi-omics integration; EMP documents one workflow for that domain without thereby closing the integration problem.
